tableware-glassware.scope_note: Glass drinking and serving ware. The glass network is the food-contact surface. Two configurations raise the stakes: LEAD CRYSTAL, in which lead oxide is a bulk constituent of the glass at up to 24 percent or more and lead release into stored acidic beverages is documented, and applied EXTERIOR ENAMEL DECORATION, which is a hand-to-mouth and lip-contact pathway rather than a fill pathway. tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.scope_note: Reusable metal drink containers. The food-contact surface is the interior alloy or its liner. The characteristic pathway is not the wall alloy but the BASE PLUG of a vacuum-insulated body, where a lead-bearing solder or braze seals the evacuation port and becomes an exposure route only if the covering cap detaches; that is the subject of well-known consumer-product recalls and Proposition 65 actions and is why the component plan requires the base to be tested and its cover retention verified as a mechanical requirement. No credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling for a metal food-contact article, so the row is a control; the Japanese and Korean percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are disclosed as MATERIAL-CONTENT companions.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.material: Single- and double-wall austenitic stainless steel and aluminium bottles and tumblers; interior lacquer or ceramic-coated liners on some aluminium bottles; vacuum-insulated bodies closed with a soldered or welded base plug; painted or powder-coated exteriors; plastic and silicone lids, straws and gaskets.
tableware-metal-bottles-tumblers.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior wall alloy, acidic-simulant release at the highest claimed hold temperature and duration; (2) interior lacquer or ceramic liner where fitted, which is a coating and takes the polymeric or ceramic regime of its own family; (3) BASE PLUG solder or braze, analysed for lead content and tested for release with the cover removed, plus a cover-retention verification; (4) threaded neck, cut edges and any weld; (5) lid, gasket, straw and bite valve, bound by the plastics migration ceilings directly or by disclosed read-across; (6) exterior paint or powder coat, tested as a mouth-and-hand-contact surface at the lip.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. On a vacuum-insulated bottle the binding component is the base-plug solder or braze, not the wall alloy; a wall-only result does not represent the article and is not accepted.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. tableware-plastic-drinkware.scope_note: Plastic drinking vessels, directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011 as articles consisting exclusively of plastics. control.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a food-contact article of any material family. This cell carries NO companion: the only sovereign tin numbers in existence are maximum levels on canned food, which are a FOOD basis on the contents of a tinplate container, and they are neither applicable to this row nor publishable as a migration ceiling. The non-detect branch therefore exists precisely because hexavalent chromium cannot be assumed absent, which makes it the hexavalent-chromium-conservative form of the requirement rather than a chromium(III)-dominated artefact. HMTc publishes the non-detect branch and declines the relaxation, and the hexavalent-chromium cell is bounded by this value. Plastic drinkware consists exclusively of plastics and is within this instrument's direct scope.

tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.name: Decorative decals/coatings on tableware
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.native_basis: element release from the glaze, enamel or glass into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE GLAZE, VITREOUS ENAMEL OR GLASS NETWORK INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined by the 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid filled-article or contact-surface extraction convention used for this material family, with decoration within 20 mm of the lip determined separately. tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.scope_note: The decoration itself, considered separately from the article it is applied to, because decoration is a distinct release surface with a distinct exposure route. Decoration that lies on an interior surface is a fill-contact pathway. Decoration within 20 mm of the lip is a LIP-CONTACT pathway, and decoration on the exterior body is a HAND-TO-MOUTH pathway; none of the three is represented by a fill extraction on an undecorated area. The applicable lead-and-cadmium release regime for applied decoration on tableware (EU 84/500/EEC and its amendments, the FDA compliance-policy guides on ceramicware and decorated glassware, and the Proposition 65 tableware consent judgments) is absent from the register, so the row is a control and the gap is recorded.
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.material: On-glaze and in-glaze ceramic enamel decals and transfers; organic overprint and lustre; applied vitreous enamel bands; gold and platinum lustre; painted and powder-coated exterior surfaces on drinkware.
tableware-decorative-decals-coatings.components: Sample and report separately: (1) each decal, enamel and lustre colour as its own lot, since release is colour-specific; (2) decoration on interior surfaces, by fill extraction; (3) decoration within 20 mm of the lip, by the lip-and-rim convention; (4) exterior body decoration, by a hand-contact wipe and extraction; (5) gold and platinum lustre and any metallic band, which additionally carry an alloy-impurity route; (6) decoration after the declared number of dishwasher cycles, because abraded and etched enamel releases more than as-supplied enamel.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is present in the HMTc regulatory register. Glazed ceramic, vitreous enamel, glass and applied decoration are governed in the real world by a dedicated lead-and-cadmium release regime (EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by 2005/31/EC for ceramic articles, and the US FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware), and by California Proposition 65 consent judgments on tableware. None of those instruments has been ingested into data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and this build refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is a control until the release regime is ingested through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway, and the gap is recorded. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. This row's unit of test is the decoration colour, not the article: each colour is a separate lot, and the three exposure routes (fill, lip and hand-to-mouth) are reported separately rather than pooled.
control.reference_method: Release testing on the filled or contact-surface article using 4 percent (v/v) acetic acid at the article's stated use temperature and duration (the release convention used for glazed, enamelled and glass food-contact articles), ICP-MS determination in the extract, with a separate determination on any decoration lying within 20 mm of the lip or on any interior decoration.

cookware-metal-alloy.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
cookware-metal-alloy.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. cookware-metal-alloy.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is bare metal or alloy. This is the alloy-leach pathway in its pure form: nickel and chromium release from austenitic stainless steel and aluminium release from bare and anodised aluminium into acidic, saline and long-simmered food are documented and material, and they are exactly the pathways for which no credible sovereign has set a release ceiling. cookware-metal-alloy.material: Bare and seasoned cast iron; austenitic stainless steel, including clad and tri-ply constructions with an aluminium or copper core; bare, anodised and spun aluminium; carbon-steel woks; riveted or welded handle attachments.
cookware-metal-alloy.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior cooking surface alloy, acidic-simulant release at the stated maximum cooking temperature and duration, third successive release governing; (2) rivets and their heads on the interior surface, which are frequently a different alloy from the body; (3) welds, brazes and any solder; (4) exposed core layer at a cut or ground rim on clad construction; (5) anodised layer integrity and the release result after the declared abrasion conditioning; (6) seasoning or factory pre-seasoning layer on cast iron and carbon steel.

cookware-metal-alloy.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. Nickel and aluminium are the operative cells on this row and are the reason it cannot borrow the plastics values: a bare austenitic stainless surface does not meet 0.02 mg/kg food nickel and a bare aluminium surface does not meet 1 mg/kg food aluminium, so importing those numbers would publish an unfounded ceiling rather than a strict one.

Nickel and aluminium are the operative cells on this row and are the reason it cannot borrow the plastics values: a bare austenitic stainless surface does not meet 0.02 mg/kg food nickel and a bare aluminium surface does not meet 1 mg/kg food aluminium, so importing those numbers would publish an unfounded ceiling rather than a strict one.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

control.rationale: Hexavalent chromium is the health-relevant chromium species and it cannot be dismissed on a metal article: chromate conversion coatings, passivation treatments and chromate-bearing pigments in interior printing are live sources, and hot alkaline conditions can oxidise chromium(III) at the surface. No credible sovereign sets a hexavalent-chromium release ceiling for a food-contact metal article, and this row's total-chromium cell is itself a control, so no published parent bounds this species and a speciation-bounded not-material determination is unavailable. The fail-safe applies. No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only). cookware-nonstick-coated.name: Nonstick-coated cookware
cookware-nonstick-coated.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
cookware-nonstick-coated.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
cookware-nonstick-coated.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is a cured fluoropolymer coating. Coatings are a Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, so the exact cell is unregulated and the published ceilings are a disclosed read-across from the plastics instrument, which is the nearest applicable sovereign value in the identical basis and is itself a fluoropolymer-compatible regime. The ceilings apply to the article as placed on market AND after the declared abrasion and thermal conditioning, because the certification question for a coated pan is whether the coating still isolates the substrate after realistic use; a pristine-coating result alone does not represent the article. Exposed interior rivets and any breached area are metal food-contact surfaces and fall to the alloy-release control regime under the component plan. This row is scoped to the ELEMENT panel; per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances are a separate and larger question that this standard does not address and does not imply anything about.
cookware-nonstick-coated.material: Fluoropolymer (PTFE and PTFE-copolymer) coating systems, usually primer plus midcoat plus topcoat, applied to spun or forged aluminium or to stainless steel; exposed stainless rivets on the interior; some reinforced with ceramic or mineral particles.
cookware-nonstick-coated.components: Sample and report separately: (1) intact coating on the cooking surface, before and after the declared abrasion and thermal-cycling conditioning; (2) exposed stainless or aluminium rivets on the interior, under the alloy-release regime; (3) deliberately scored or abraded coating representing end-of-life, to expose the substrate contribution; (4) exposed substrate at the rim and any cut edge; (5) coating pigment and any ceramic or mineral reinforcement; (6) primer layer, tested where the topcoat is thin enough not to constitute a functional barrier.

cookware-ceramic-coated.name: Ceramic-coated cookware
cookware-ceramic-coated.native_basis: element release from the glaze, enamel or glass into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)

cookware-ceramic-coated.scope_note: Cookware whose food-contact surface is an INORGANIC coating: a sol-gel or vitreous enamel layer rather than a polymer. The row is therefore a control and the gap is recorded; the plastics migration limits are not substituted, because a fired inorganic coating and a polymer film are different material families extracted by different methods. Coloured enamel interiors are the configuration of concern, since frit colourants are the element source.

cookware-ceramic-coated.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior enamel or sol-gel cooking surface, 4 percent acetic acid release at the stated maximum cooking temperature and duration; (2) each interior enamel colour as its own lot; (3) enamel after the declared abrasion and thermal-shock conditioning, and at any chip, craze or spall; (4) exposed rim, cut edge and any ground area where the substrate is bare; (5) rivets and handle attachments on the interior; (6) exterior enamel where it can contact food during pouring or serving.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign release ceiling for this material family is present in the HMTc regulatory register. Glazed ceramic, vitreous enamel, glass and applied decoration are governed in the real world by a dedicated lead-and-cadmium release regime (EU Council Directive 84/500/EEC as amended by 2005/31/EC for ceramic articles, and the US FDA compliance-policy guides on lead in ceramicware and decorated glassware), and by California Proposition 65 consent judgments on tableware. None of those instruments has been ingested into data/evidence/regulatory_limits.csv, and this build refuses to substitute the plastics specific migration limits for a glaze-release limit: the two are different extractions on different material families and the substitution would be a basis conflation. The cell is a control until the release regime is ingested through the verified regulatory-fetch pathway, and the gap is recorded. Lead is the dominant pathway for this material family: lead-fluxed and lead-bisilicate glazes, lead-bearing on-glaze enamels and applied decoration, and under-fired or acid-attacked glaze surfaces all release lead into acidic food. It is the single cell where the absent release regime matters most, and the gap is recorded rather than papered over with a plastics value. Ceramic-coated and enamelled cookware sits in the glaze-release family rather than the plastics family, so it inherits this family's absent regime; coloured interior enamel is tested colour by colour and after abrasion and thermal-shock conditioning.

bakeware.name: Bakeware
bakeware.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
bakeware.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. bakeware.scope_note: Bakeware in its principal configuration, which is a metal pan with or without a release coating, so the row takes the metal-article release control regime. Two features distinguish it from stovetop cookware and are written into the component plan: baking is a DRY, high-temperature, long-duration contact, which is not the acidic-simulant condition the standard migration conventions were designed around, so the release test must be run at the stated baking temperature and the acidic condition retained only for acidic batters and fruit fillings; and disposable aluminium foil pans are single-use bare aluminium in direct contact with acidic fillings. Glass, ceramic and silicone bakeware are separate material families whose own regimes apply to those components and configurations.
bakeware.material: Aluminised and tinned steel, bare and anodised aluminium, and carbon-steel pans; non-stick and silicone-release coated bakeware; glass and ceramic baking dishes; moulded silicone bakeware; disposable aluminium foil pans.
bakeware.components: Sample and report separately: (1) interior pan surface alloy or coating, release tested at the stated maximum baking temperature and duration; (2) acidic-filling configuration, tested against an acidic simulant at baking temperature; (3) release coating before and after the declared abrasion and thermal-cycling conditioning; (4) tinned or aluminised layer integrity and the exposed steel substrate at any scratch or cut edge; (5) disposable foil pans as their own lot; (6) glass, ceramic and silicone configurations under their own material-family regimes, reported separately and never pooled with the metal result.

bakeware.basis_guard: element release from the food-contact alloy into food
bakeware.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. Bakeware release testing must be run at the stated baking temperature and duration rather than only at the ambient acidic-simulant convention, because dry high-temperature contact is this row's actual use condition.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

cookware-specialty-alloy.name: Specialty alloy cookware (copper, carbon steel)
cookware-specialty-alloy.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
cookware-specialty-alloy.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. cookware-specialty-alloy.scope_note: Cookware in alloy families whose impurity and constituent profiles differ materially from stainless and aluminium, which is why the taxonomy splits it out. cookware-specialty-alloy.material: Copper pans, lined with tin or stainless steel or unlined; brass and bronze cooking and serving vessels; carbon-steel woks, crepe and paella pans; silver- and nickel-plated serving ware; unlined copper preserving pans.
cookware-specialty-alloy.components: Sample and report separately: (1) tin lining, acidic-simulant release at the stated cooking conditions, and the exposed copper at any worn-through area; (2) unlined copper or brass food-contact surface, with alloy composition verified for lead, arsenic and antimony; (3) cast fittings, handles and rivets, verified for leaded-brass composition; (4) plated surfaces, tested intact and at any worn or flaked area, with the substrate alloy identified; (5) brazes and solders at seams and handle joins; (6) re-tinned or repaired articles as their own lot.

not_material.rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains. not_material.reference_method: Total-mercury release determination per the tHg control; reflex methylmercury speciation by GC-ICP-MS only where total mercury is detected in the release extract.
not_material.regulatory_basis: No credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for a food-contact material or article in any basis. The metallic mercury impurity route in an alloy produces no organomercury species.

Plastic boards are within this instrument's direct scope; wooden and bamboo boards have no specific measure in any credible jurisdiction and take the same values by disclosed read-across.

not_material.rationale: Inorganic arsenic is a dietary speciation with no separate food-contact-material instrument anywhere in the credible set: every food-contact element requirement is written on total arsenic. Arsenic migrating from a polymeric food-contact article is in any case inorganic, so the total-arsenic non-detect requirement is simultaneously the tightest achievable inorganic-arsenic ceiling and bounds this cell by identity. No separate inorganic-arsenic ceiling is published, and inorganic arsenic never substitutes for the total-arsenic cell.
not_material.bounded_by: tAs (eu_10_2011_tas_sml_nd, total arsenic not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food)
not_material.reference_method: Total-arsenic migration determination per the tAs cell; reflex inorganic-arsenic speciation by HPLC-ICP-MS on the migration extract only where total arsenic is detected at or above the detection limit.
not_material.regulatory_basis: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 sets the element requirement as a specific migration requirement on the food or food simulant, not as a limit on the material's element content. No credible sovereign sets a species-specific migration limit for this cell.

Ni.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 1: nickel specific migration limit 0.02 mg/kg food
Ni.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Ni.substantiation: Nickel carries a positive specific migration limit of 0.02 mg/kg food, the tightest positive SML in the Annex II element list. Plastic boards are within this instrument's direct scope; wooden and bamboo boards have no specific measure in any credible jurisdiction and take the same values by disclosed read-across. This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface only; where a food-contact component of the article is a nickel-bearing alloy, that component sits in the alloy-release control regime described in this row's component plan, because the plastics SML was not written for and is not achievable by a bare stainless-steel surface.

control.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a food-contact article of any material family. Tin is nonetheless a mandatory panel cell, because tin stabilisers in PVC compounds and tin-bearing solder are live pathways in parts of this category, so it is tested on every certified lot with no invented ceiling. This cell carries NO companion: the only sovereign tin numbers in existence are maximum levels on canned food, which are a FOOD basis on the contents of a tinplate container, and they are neither applicable to this row nor publishable as a migration ceiling. They are named as a companion only on the rows where a tinplate or crown component actually exists.
control.reference_method: EN 1186 / EN 13130 food-simulant migration testing on the finished article under its worst foreseeable use conditions (simulant, temperature and contact time selected per Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III and Annex V; for repeat-use articles the third successive migration result governs), with ICP-MS determination of the element in the simulant.

Cr.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: total chromium not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.01 mg/kg food; the 3.6 mg/kg food relaxation available on documented exclusion of chromium(VI) is declined
Cr.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Cr.substantiation: This total-chromium cell is deliberately published as a firm ceiling rather than the usual non-protective total-chromium screen, and the reason is structural to the instrument. Annex II point 2 as amended by Reg (EU) 2020/1245 sets total chromium at not detectable and permits a relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food limit only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. HMTc publishes the non-detect branch and declines the relaxation, and the hexavalent-chromium cell is bounded by this value. Plastic boards are within this instrument's direct scope; wooden and bamboo boards have no specific measure in any credible jurisdiction and take the same values by disclosed read-across.

not_material.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 controls hexavalent chromium through the total-chromium requirement rather than through a separate species limit: total chromium must be not detectable, and the relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food value becomes available only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. HMTc declines that relaxation, so every certified article is held to total chromium not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food, which bounds hexavalent chromium at or below the same value. No credible sovereign sets a hexavalent-chromium migration limit for a food-contact material, so no separate species ceiling is published; hexavalent chromium never substitutes for the total-chromium cell.

food-prep-blender-jars.name: Blender jars
food-prep-blender-jars.native_basis: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food), Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II convention
food-prep-blender-jars.native_basis_label: specific element migration INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT from the polymeric food-contact surface, µg/kg of food, determined by the Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III to V simulant, temperature and contact-time conventions. This is a MIGRATION basis and not a total-content basis: no cell on this row limits how much of an element the material CONTAINS, and no cell on this row is expressed per kg of material.
food-prep-blender-jars.scope_note: The removable jar and its blade assembly. The principal food-contact material of the modern jar body is a plastic consisting exclusively of plastics, directly within Reg (EU) 10/2011, so the published ceilings anchor that instrument. GLASS jar bodies are a separate material family whose release regime is absent from the register and are handled under the component plan by the glass-and-glaze control regime, reported separately. The STAINLESS BLADE ASSEMBLY is the component that distinguishes this row from a plastic tub: blending is high-shear, abrasive and often hot, the blade and collar are alloy in direct contact, and the shaft seal and bearing can shed, so the blade assembly is tested under the alloy-release regime with abrasion conditioning rather than represented by a jar-body result.
food-prep-blender-jars.material: Tritan copolyester, SAN, polycarbonate and polypropylene jars; soda-lime and borosilicate glass jars; stainless-steel blade assemblies with a bearing, shaft seal and swaged or threaded collar; elastomer gaskets and drive couplers.
food-prep-blender-jars.components: Sample and report separately: (1) plastic jar body interior at the third successive migration and at the highest claimed contact temperature; (2) glass jar bodies as their own lot under the glass-and-glaze control regime; (3) STAINLESS BLADE, collar and swage, alloy-release tested after the declared abrasion and hot-blending conditioning; (4) shaft seal, bearing and any lubricant that can reach product; (5) lid, plug and gasket components; (6) printed graduations on an interior surface.
food-prep-blender-jars.audit_scope: food.contact|food contact|plastic food|utensil|cookware|cooking utensil|kitchen|tableware|crockery|ceramic|porcelain|earthenware|glaze|enamel|glassware|hollowware|packaging and containers|food-contact surface
food-prep-blender-jars.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis.

not_material.rationale: Methylmercury is formed by microbial methylation in aquatic food chains. A cured polymer, a fired glaze, a metal alloy and a coated article contain no methylation pathway, and no credible sovereign sets a methylmercury requirement for any food-contact material. The total-mercury non-detect requirement bounds any organomercury fraction that could be present. No separate methylmercury ceiling is published, and methylmercury never substitutes for the total-mercury cell.

Ni.substantiation: Nickel carries a positive specific migration limit of 0.02 mg/kg food, the tightest positive SML in the Annex II element list. control.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II lists no tin entry, and no credible sovereign sets a tin migration or release ceiling for a food-contact article of any material family. Tin is nonetheless a mandatory panel cell, because tin stabilisers in PVC compounds and tin-bearing solder are live pathways in parts of this category, so it is tested on every certified lot with no invented ceiling. This cell carries NO companion: the only sovereign tin numbers in existence are maximum levels on canned food, which are a FOOD basis on the contents of a tinplate container, and they are neither applicable to this row nor publishable as a migration ceiling. They are named as a companion only on the rows where a tinplate or crown component actually exists.
control.reference_method: EN 1186 / EN 13130 food-simulant migration testing on the finished article under its worst foreseeable use conditions (simulant, temperature and contact time selected per Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex III and Annex V; for repeat-use articles the third successive migration result governs), with ICP-MS determination of the element in the simulant.

Al.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 1: aluminium specific migration limit 1 mg/kg food

This value governs the polymeric food-contact surface; it is not applied to an aluminium metal article, because an instrument written for plastics did not contemplate an article whose food-contact surface is the element itself.

Cr.label: Reg (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2: total chromium not detectable in the food or simulant, detection limit 0.01 mg/kg food; the 3.6 mg/kg food relaxation available on documented exclusion of chromium(VI) is declined
Cr.basis_label: specific element migration into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
Cr.substantiation: This total-chromium cell is deliberately published as a firm ceiling rather than the usual non-protective total-chromium screen, and the reason is structural to the instrument. Annex II point 2 as amended by Reg (EU) 2020/1245 sets total chromium at not detectable and permits a relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food limit only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. The non-detect branch therefore exists precisely because hexavalent chromium cannot be assumed absent, which makes it the hexavalent-chromium-conservative form of the requirement rather than a chromium(III)-dominated artefact. HMTc publishes the non-detect branch and declines the relaxation, and the hexavalent-chromium cell is bounded by this value. The bowl and lid consist exclusively of plastics and are within this instrument's direct scope; the stainless cutting components are reported under the alloy-release regime in the component plan.

not_material.rationale: Regulation (EU) 10/2011 Annex II point 2 controls hexavalent chromium through the total-chromium requirement rather than through a separate species limit: total chromium must be not detectable, and the relaxed 3.6 mg/kg food value becomes available only where the operator documents that chromium(VI) is absent. HMTc declines that relaxation, so every certified article is held to total chromium not detectable at 0.01 mg/kg food, which bounds hexavalent chromium at or below the same value. No credible sovereign sets a hexavalent-chromium migration limit for a food-contact material, so no separate species ceiling is published; hexavalent chromium never substitutes for the total-chromium cell.

food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.name: Coffee-maker pathways
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. This is a RELEASE basis on the food, not the plastics-simulant convention and not a total-content basis: the percent-by-weight lead limits on food-contact metals and solder are a separate MATERIAL-CONTENT obligation, disclosed as companions and never published here.
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.scope_note: The full WETTED PATHWAY of a beverage-brewing appliance, from reservoir to cup, taken as a system rather than as a single material. The row is a control because the pathway is dominated by components in material families for which no credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling: aluminium and copper boilers, brass and leaded-brass fittings and group heads, and plated wetted parts. Two conditions make this row harsher than a storage article and are written into the component plan: the water is HOT and often near-boiling and is held in contact with the boiler and fittings, and DESCALING with acid is a manufacturer-instructed periodic condition that strips passivation and mobilises metal, so the release test must include a post-descaling draw. Polymeric reservoirs, carafes and tubing are bound by the plastics migration ceilings directly or by disclosed read-across as separate components, and the sovereign drinking-water parametric values are disclosed as WATER-basis companions on the beverage, never as this row's release ceilings.
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.material: Plastic water reservoirs and carafe bodies; silicone and EPDM tubing; aluminium and copper boilers and thermoblocks; brass and leaded-brass fittings, valves and group heads; stainless steel heater tubes and portafilters; nickel-plated and chrome-plated wetted parts; aluminium moka pots.
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.components: Sample and report separately: (1) first-draw and steady-state brewed-water sampling through the assembled appliance, against a matched influent blank; (2) BOILER or thermoblock interior, aluminium and copper configurations as their own lots; (3) BRASS and leaded-brass fittings, valves and group heads, alloy composition verified for lead; (4) POST-DESCALING draw, sampled immediately after the manufacturer's stated descaling procedure and again after the stated flush; (5) silicone and EPDM tubing, under the polymer regime by disclosed read-across; (6) plastic reservoir and carafe, under the plastics migration ceilings; (7) plated and stainless wetted parts, including any solder or braze; (8) aluminium moka pots and stovetop brewers as their own lot.

food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.basis_guard: element release from the food-contact alloy into food
food-prep-coffee-maker-pathways.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap.

control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 governs plastics only; metals and alloys are a separate Regulation 1935/2004 Annex I material family for which the EU has adopted no specific measure, the US regulates food-contact substances without an element release ceiling, and Codex, FSANZ, Health Canada, the UK and Hong Kong set none. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. Both jurisdictions also sit OUTSIDE the HMTc credible-regulator set used for anchoring in this build, so they could not supply a published number here even in the right basis; they are disclosed as real foreign obligations and must not be promoted to anchors without a recorded governance ruling. That obligation is disclosed as a companion and is verified on every certified article; it is not published as this row's release ceiling, because a content limit and a release limit are different measured quantities. The binding component on this row is normally a brass fitting or an aluminium or copper boiler, and the binding CONDITION is the post-descaling draw; a cold-reservoir or first-brew result does not represent the appliance.
control.reference_method: Food-simulant release testing on each food-contact metal component under worst foreseeable use conditions (acidic simulant at the article's stated cooking or holding temperature and duration; for repeat-use articles the third successive release result governs), ICP-MS determination in the simulant, plus alloy-composition verification of every food-contact component by ICP-OES after acid digestion (XRF for screening only).

food-prep-kettle-interiors.name: Kettle interiors
food-prep-kettle-interiors.native_basis: element release from the food-contact alloy into food or food simulant (µg/kg food)
food-prep-kettle-interiors.native_basis_label: element RELEASE FROM THE FOOD-CONTACT ALLOY INTO FOOD OR A FOOD SIMULANT, µg/kg of food, determined against an acidic simulant at the article's stated use temperature and duration with the third successive release governing for repeat-use articles. food-prep-kettle-interiors.scope_note: The interior wetted surface of an electric or stovetop kettle, taken at BOILING as the operative condition. The row is a control because the characteristic components sit in material families with no sovereign element release ceiling: the exposed heating element and its boss, brass and plated fittings, and welded seams. Boiling water contact is a harsher extraction than any of the standard food-simulant conventions and is the condition the test must use; repeated boil-dry cycles and periodic acid descaling are additional required conditionings. control.rationale: No credible sovereign sets a numeric ceiling on element release from a metal or alloy food-contact article. Testing is therefore mandatory on every certified lot with no invented ceiling: a limit borrowed from the plastics regulation would be a limit written for a different material family, and for an alloy surface the plastics nickel and aluminium values are not even achievable, so borrowing them would be an unfounded number rather than a stricter one. Lead in a food-contact metal article arrives from the alloy, from lead-bearing solder and brazing at joints and base plugs, and from plated or printed decoration on the interior. Japan Notice 370 (1959) and Korea MFDS Notice 2024-29 do set sovereign lead limits for food-contact metals, but they are percent-by-weight limits on the metal, solder and tin plating: a MATERIAL-CONTENT basis. water-filters.name: Water filters
water-filters.native_basis: element release from the treatment device into the treated water (µg/L, reported as µg/kg)
water-filters.native_basis_label: NET ELEMENT RELEASE FROM THE TREATMENT DEVICE INTO THE TREATED WATER, µg/L reported as µg/kg, determined as device effluent minus a matched influent blank so that any contribution BY the device is resolved separately from what the device removes. This is a device-release basis on the water leaving the device; the sovereign drinking-water parametric values are a WATER basis on the supply as delivered and are disclosed as companions, never republished as the device's release ceiling.
water-filters.scope_note: The assembled point-of-use treatment device. This row must be scoped honestly in both directions, because a filter is an INTERVENTION WHOSE PURPOSE IS TO REMOVE METALS: the certification question is not only whether treated water meets a limit, which the influent may already have done, but whether the device itself CONTRIBUTES any element to the water it treats, and separately whether it delivers the reduction it claims across its rated life. Both are mandatory determinations here. No credible sovereign sets an element release ceiling for a treatment device, so the row is a control; the EU Directive 2020/2184 route is an Art. 11 hygiene-and-positive-list regime rather than element release values, the US route is the SDWA lead-free content definition plus NSF/ANSI 61 conformity, and neither is in the register. Sovereign drinking-water parametric values are disclosed as WATER-basis companions on the treated water and are never republished as the device's release ceiling. A device must never be credited for the influent's cleanliness, and reduction performance must never be inferred from a low effluent result on clean influent.
water-filters.material: Pitcher, faucet-mount, under-sink, gravity and reverse-osmosis point-of-use devices; plastic housings and reservoirs; activated-carbon block and granular media; ion-exchange resin; KDF-type copper-zinc redox alloy; activated alumina; ceramic elements; RO membranes; metal and plastic wetted fittings, tubing and taps.
water-filters.components: Sample and report separately: (1) NET CONTRIBUTION, effluent minus matched influent blank, at first draw, after the manufacturer's conditioning volume, at 50 percent of rated capacity and at 100 percent of rated capacity; (2) REDUCTION PERFORMANCE against a spiked challenge influent for every element the device claims to reduce, reported at end of rated life rather than when new; (3) housing, reservoir and lid polymer, under the plastics migration ceilings directly or by disclosed read-across; (4) metal wetted fittings, taps, tubing connectors and any solder or leaded brass, under the alloy-release regime; (5) end-of-life and past-rated-capacity behaviour, including any release of accumulated element load from loaded media; (6) stagnation draw after the longest stand time the instructions permit.

control.rationale: A drinking-water treatment device is an intervention whose purpose is to REMOVE metals, so the certification question is not whether the effluent meets a food limit but whether the device itself contributes any element to the water it treats. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory net-contribution testing against a matched influent blank, and the sovereign drinking-water parametric value is disclosed as a companion obligation in the WATER basis, never republished as a device release ceiling. Lead is the element a filter is most often bought to remove, and it is simultaneously a possible device contribution from leaded brass fittings, bronze bodies and soldered joints in the wetted path. filter-media-and-housings.name: Filter media and housings
filter-media-and-housings.native_basis: element release from the treatment device into the treated water (µg/L, reported as µg/kg)
filter-media-and-housings.native_basis_label: NET ELEMENT RELEASE FROM THE TREATMENT DEVICE INTO THE TREATED WATER, µg/L reported as µg/kg, determined as device effluent minus a matched influent blank so that any contribution BY the device is resolved separately from what the device removes. This is a device-release basis on the water leaving the device; the sovereign drinking-water parametric values are a WATER basis on the supply as delivered and are disclosed as companions, never republished as the device's release ceiling.
filter-media-and-housings.scope_note: The media and housing components sold and replaced separately from the device. The media cell is unregulated in a way worth stating precisely: Reg (EU) 10/2011 does not merely omit ion-exchange resin, it EXPRESSLY EXCLUDES it by Art. 2(2)(a), and there is no EU specific measure for adsorbent media of any kind. Media are also the component that carries an inherent element load, since KDF-type media are a copper-zinc alloy, activated alumina is an aluminium compound, and mineral adsorbents carry raw-material impurities, so an unconditioned first draw from fresh media is the expected worst case and the conditioning instruction is part of what is certified. Plastic housings, sumps and end caps are within the plastics migration ceilings as separate components. Spent media additionally hold the element load they removed, so change-out interval and end-of-life behaviour are certified requirements rather than advisory.
filter-media-and-housings.material: Activated carbon, granular and block, coconut- and coal-based; ion-exchange resin, cation and anion; KDF-type copper-zinc redox alloy; activated alumina; iron-oxide and titanium-oxide adsorbents; diatomaceous earth and ceramic elements; RO and UF membranes with polysulfone supports; plastic cartridge housings, sumps, end caps, O-rings and manifolds.
filter-media-and-housings.components: Sample and report separately: (1) each MEDIUM as its own lot, extraction at first draw and after the stated conditioning volume, against a matched influent blank; (2) KDF-type copper-zinc alloy media, with alloy composition verified for lead, cadmium and nickel impurity; (3) activated alumina and aluminium-bearing media, tested specifically for aluminium net contribution; (4) mineral, ceramic and diatomaceous media, tested for arsenic and heavy-metal raw-material load; (5) ION-EXCHANGE RESIN, expressly outside Reg (EU) 10/2011 by Art. 2(2)(a), tested for both element release and resin-fine carryover; (6) plastic housing, sump, end cap, O-ring and manifold, under the plastics migration ceilings; (7) SPENT media at and beyond rated capacity, for release of accumulated element load; (8) any metal insert, mesh, spring or fitting in the wetted path.

filter-media-and-housings.basis_guard_note: Only an instrument expressed as specific element migration into food or a food simulant may anchor a cell on this row. The guard exists to reject the three foreign bases that surround this category and would otherwise look plausible: the FOOD basis (canned-food tin maximum levels, which limit the contents and not the article), the MATERIAL-CONTENT basis (CPSIA total lead in substrate, EU REACH Annex XVII cadmium percent-by-weight restrictions, RoHS homogeneous-material limits, Japan Notice 370 and Korea MFDS percent-by-weight lead in food-contact metals), and the ARTICLE-EXTRACTION basis of the toy regime (EU 2009/48 Annex II Part III and ASTM F963 soluble limits, which are element migration from scraped-off or coated TOY material into 0.07 M hydrochloric acid, expressed per kg of MATERIAL, not per kg of food). Any of those would fail this guard and resolve to a gap rather than publish in the wrong basis. On this control row the guard is declaratory as well as operative: it records the only basis in which a future ingested instrument would be allowed to supply this row's numbers, so that a content limit, a food limit, a water limit or a plastics specific migration limit cannot later be dropped in as this row's release ceiling. The plastics clause is deliberately absent from this guard: a Reg (EU) 10/2011 value named here would fail the guard and resolve to a gap.

No credible sovereign sets a release ceiling for a treatment device or its media: the EU regulates materials in contact with water intended for human consumption through the Art. 11 hygiene-requirement and positive-list route of Directive (EU) 2020/2184 rather than through element release values, the US route is the SDWA lead-free content definition plus NSF/ANSI 61 conformity, and neither is a sovereign element release ceiling in this register. Regulation (EU) 10/2011 does not reach the media at all: Art. 2(2)(a) expressly excludes ion exchange resins from its scope. The cell is therefore a control with mandatory net-contribution testing against a matched influent blank, and the sovereign drinking-water parametric value is disclosed as a companion obligation in the WATER basis, never republished as a device release ceiling.
control.reference_method: Device-effluent extraction testing on the conditioned device: influent of defined composition passed through the device at rated flow, effluent sampled at first draw, after the manufacturer's conditioning volume, and at rated capacity, with ICP-MS determination of each element in the effluent and comparison against the matched influent blank so that any net contribution by the device is resolved separately from what the device removes. Hexavalent-chromium speciation by ion-chromatography ICP-MS on both effluent and matched influent, per EPA Method 218.7 conventions.
